title: Sparsh Dadhich
description: Embedded ML for medical sensing. Bioimpedance instruments, sensor data-acquisition hardware and firmware, and ML that runs on microcontrollers.
name: Sparsh Dadhich

featured.title: TPT-Finder bioimpedance instrument
text: Bioimpedance boards for a pen-like surgical probe that tells thyroid from parathyroid tissue in real time. I ran the ex-vivo study and all 500+ tissue measurements on the two-electrode BioZ v2, then designed the four-electrode BioZ v4.
I designed BioZ v4 as Biomedical Instrumentation & Impedance Lead at the UW BioRobotics Lab.

featured.title: Project SHIELD: sensor DAQ board and stress-test rig
text: An ESP32-S3 data-acquisition board for 8 sensor types, built for about $1,700 of a $4,000 sponsor budget, plus the rig that stress-tests it.
Co-hardware lead (with Thomas Glass) and procurement lead on the capstone; at ARC Lab I lead the stress-test campaign and built the rig automation.

key.label: sensor types on one DAQ board

featured.title: BackOnTrack: wearable posture monitor
text: A wearable posture monitor whose on-device classifier got 95 of 100 live movements right in an informal check.
I wrote all of the firmware for a four-person EE/BIOEN 461 course team.

featured.title: SmartCrib: on-device infant cry detector
text: An infant-cry detector that runs fully on an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense; the INT8 model is 41% smaller than float32 with the same test results.
Joint project with Jonathan Lu, built as the EE/CSE 474 final project.

featured.title: Real-time EMG BCI
text: An EMG-driven cursor with a Kalman filter; successful reaches fell from 10–16 to 2–4 of 19 as the added feedback lag rose from ≈0–125 ms to ≈360–590 ms.

*Built for EE 466 (Winter 2026) at UW in a three-person lab group with Jonathan and Olivia, following the course protocol and script outlines by A. L. Orsborn. The code here and the lag-sweep analysis are my own.*

approach.heading: Approach
approach.headline: From noisy signal to trusted decision.
body: Across my projects I've worked every stage between the two: a breadboard prototype, the board, the firmware that samples it, the analysis that checks the data, and the model that runs on the microcontroller. Knowing the whole chain is how I find where a signal goes wrong.
